source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor
finding: Next-token loss over a context equals the prequential code length. So training an in-context learner minimizes data fit plus the complexity of the model inferred from context.
numbers: Theory plus meta-learned sequence-model experiments on regression, sinusoid and Mastermind tasks; prequential ICL beat past-token (train-risk) ICL on all tasks.
limits: Gap is largest at short contexts and shrinks with data. Normative account shown on small synthetic meta-datasets, not on LLM benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Few-example reading already favours simple explanations, but this is not reliable without a check.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor (SGD comparison)
finding: A standard SGD learner fits more complex functions and generalizes worse than prequential ICL when data is scarce. With enough data the advantage vanishes.
numbers: Fig. 2: ICL has lower prequential code length in low-data regimes on all tasks; regularized SGD still beaten in low data.
limits: Advantage tied to low data. Architecture matters: only the non-bottleneck Transformer did well on Mastermind; state-space models won on the HMM task.
agent_relevance: The agent works in the few-example regime, where the complexity preference is strongest.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor (pretrained GPT-4 test)
finding: Section 3.4 prompted GPT-4 with a Mastermind description plus in-context examples and read logits. The paper says current ICL methods can still struggle to minimize prequential code length on a novel task.
numbers: Compared against a naive baseline; exact GPT-4 figures not extracted this session.
limits: Single task; qualitative only.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a pretrained LLM is a good MDL learner on a new task; check with code.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression
finding: Large LLMs used with arithmetic coding are strong general compressors, even on images and audio never seen in text training.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B: ImageNet patches 43.4% of raw size vs PNG 58.5%; LibriSpeech 16.4% vs FLAC 30.3%; enwik9 raw rate 8.3% (Table 1, 1 GB datasets, 2048-byte chunks).
limits: Raw rate ignores model size.
agent_relevance: Shows why a hypothesis must be charged its own size.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression (adjusted rates)
finding: When model size is counted (two-part code), foundation models lose to gzip/LZMA on small data and win only when data is large. Models trained on enwik8 overfit to Wikipedia.
numbers: Table 1 adjusted rate: Chinchilla rows exceed 100% on ImageNet, LibriSpeech and random data; gzip enwik9 32.3%, ImageNet 70.7%. Larger models help only on larger datasets (Fig. 2).
limits: I could not read every cell of the garbled table; claim limited to the direction.
agent_relevance: Parameters count as hypothesis length; the tie-break must charge for hypothesis size, not only fit.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly
finding: Across 31 public LLMs and 12 benchmarks, bits per character on external corpora correlate almost linearly with average benchmark score.
numbers: Pearson about -0.93, RMSE 3.1% on the average score; HellaSwag -0.881, TriviaQA -0.951, MMLU -0.890; coding benchmarks within [-1,-0.9], DS-1000 -0.946; math average -0.930.
limits: Holds when the corpus matches the domain; some models flagged as outliers likely overfit to benchmarks. Correlation across models, not within one model's answers.
agent_relevance: Compression tracks general ability across models. It does not say how to choose between two answers from one model, so do not use it as a per-answer judge.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly (domain match)
finding: The linear fit is much weaker when the compression corpus does not match the benchmark domain.
numbers: Authors report the out-of-domain correlation as significantly weaker than in-domain (e.g. maths vs knowledge corpora).
limits: Small set of mostly open-weight models.
agent_relevance: Description-length comparisons need a matched code or prior.

source: Voita and Titov (2020) Information-Theoretic Probing with MDL
finding: Probe quality measured as codelength of labels given representations, including the probe's own cost (online and variational codes).
numbers: Table 2 (POS, kbits, variational): layer 0 linguistic 85 vs control 470; accuracy at layer 0 was 93.7 linguistic vs 96.3 control, so accuracy favours the control task while codelength does not. Control codelengths at least twice linguistic.
limits: Main table covers one pretrained encoder family. Variational and online codes give different absolute values, same trends.
agent_relevance: MDL fixes a case where fit accuracy rewards memorization. Matches G3: fitting the given data is not proof.
quote: codelength is able to distinguish these tasks without any search for settings

source: Voita and Titov (2020) Information-Theoretic Probing with MDL (model vs data code)
finding: Control-task probes need a model code several times larger than genuine linguistic probes; the data code alone cannot show it.
numbers: Fig. 2a: model component several times larger for control tasks. Contextual encoders with random weights still much better than embeddings alone.
limits: Choice of code changes absolute lengths.
agent_relevance: Report hypothesis cost and data cost separately in any tie-break so memorization is visible.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The Description Length of Deep Learning Models
finding: Prequential (online) coding of deep networks gives far better compression than variational two-part codes, which are poor despite being built to minimize the bound.
numbers: MNIST: prequential codelength 4.10 kbits (ratio 0.021) with 99.5% test accuracy vs best variational 24.1 kbits (ratio 0.12) at 95.5%. CIFAR10: 45.3 kbits (ratio 0.27), about 93% test accuracy.
limits: Depends on the chosen incremental code. Networks can reach 100% training accuracy on random labels.
agent_relevance: Online code idea gives a cheap MDL score: score a hypothesis by how well it predicts each next case in order.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Self-Adaptive In-Context Learning: An Information Compression Perspective
finding: Chooses in-context example sets by minimum codelength of the test label given context, after TopK retrieval.
numbers: GPT2-XL, 8 NLP datasets, average accuracy: TopK+MDL 60.16 vs TopK 58.14 (3.48% relative), TopK+LocalE 51.36, Majority vote 50.43, Random 43.06 (40.41% relative gap). Abstract: 40% relative gain.
limits: Codelength uses model confidence, which is entropy minimization. Small model.
agent_relevance: Confidence-based MDL picks the most confident, not necessarily the most correct. Weak tie-break only; conflicts with G4 and G5 if treated as proof.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Self-Adaptive In-Context Learning: An Information Compression Perspective (what the score is)
finding: Section 4.4 says the codelength term reduces to entropy of the model's output when confidence is used as the distribution.
numbers: Minimizing L(y|c,x) is equal to searching for examples that make the model confident.
limits: No separate hypothesis-length term beyond the example set.
agent_relevance: Label such a score as confidence unless a real model-length term is counted.

source: Kolmogorov-Test authors (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation
finding: Asks code LLMs for the shortest program that outputs a given sequence. Frontier models do poorly.
numbers: Prompted Llama-3.1-405B and GPT-4o err on more than 78% and 40% of natural sequences and more than 65% and 55% of synthetic ones. Generated programs are larger than gzip output on average (Precision above 1.0).
limits: Program length measured after gzip as prior. Gains on synthetic data generalize poorly to real audio, text, DNA.
agent_relevance: LLM-written short programs are weak compressors; a model's own claims of simplicity are unreliable, so count length in code.

source: Kolmogorov-Test authors (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation (trained model)
finding: Fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B (SeqCoder) reaches lower compression rates than earlier approaches on the synthetic distribution and sometimes beats gzip; inline execution feedback gives modest gains.
numbers: Tables 1-2 give Accuracy and Precision per modality; exact cells not extracted here.
limits: Does not carry to real data.
agent_relevance: Execution feedback helps only slightly; the exact check is still needed.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: A 76K-parameter network, no pretraining, trained at inference time only on the target puzzle to minimize its description length, solves a fifth of ARC-AGI-1 evaluation puzzles.
numbers: 20% of evaluation and 34.75% of training puzzles with 2 guesses, 2000 steps, about 20 min per puzzle on an RTX 4070. Compare: 87.5% for large pretrained LLM pipelines (semi-private); 40.3% for ARC-data-trained HRM ablation; U-Net baseline 0.75%.
limits: Appendix lists abilities it cannot do. Heavy compute per puzzle.
agent_relevance: Cleanest working MDL solver on reasoning puzzles; a description-length score alone reaches non-trivial accuracy without a language model.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) (compute curve)
finding: Accuracy keeps rising with inference-time steps.
numbers: Evaluation set, pass@1: 100 steps 0.75%; 500 steps 13.5%; 1000 steps 16.75%; 1500 steps 18.25%. Training set pass@1: 1000 steps 28%, 2000 steps 30.25%.
limits: Pass@n columns not mapped exactly here.
agent_relevance: MDL minimization needs real search budget.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: GPT-4 proposes natural-language hypotheses, each becomes code and is checked on the training pairs. Summarizing hypotheses shrank the pool.
numbers: 100 random ARC tasks: Direct 17%, Program Only 23%, Summarized Hypotheses 30%, Human-Selected 33%, Human-Written 45%. GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks; 28 of the 30 solved had one.
limits: No explicit description-length term.
agent_relevance: Same propose-then-filter pattern as the schema. The missing piece is a simplicity score to rank survivors.

source: Singhal et al. (2026) LLM Priors for ERM over Programs (LLM-PV)
finding: Propose-and-verify: an LLM proposes short programs, each is scored on held-out validation data, best kept, no gradients.
numbers: 200 labeled examples at length 10 give 100% test accuracy on tasks such as 10-parity, CAP and IsPrime where SGD stays near chance even with 100k examples; shifted primality IsPrime+47 reaches 80.6% at n=100.
limits: SHA-256 parity stays near chance for all methods.
agent_relevance: Supports G3: select among short programs by held-out data, not by fit to the given examples.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder
finding: Library learning with an explicit Bayesian/MDL compression objective: refactor solved programs and add reusable primitives.
numbers: Beats memorize-only baselines and enumeration (up to 400 million programs per task, 24 h); in LOGO graphics and tower building no alternative solves over 60% of held-out tasks while DreamCoder nears 100%.
limits: Training takes about a day on 20-100 CPUs. Compression gain is tangled with the neural recognition model (both ablated, both help).
agent_relevance: Classic AI system using MDL to choose abstractions; supports compressing past solutions into reusable operators.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum Description Length Revisited
finding: MDL model selection is typically consistent but behaves like BIC: consistent, not prediction-optimal.
numbers: Text: MDL and Bayes factors behave like BIC for large n; AIC-like methods have the reverse trade-off; Yang (2005) shows the tension in general.
limits: Consistency needs the true distribution in the model class; misspecification needs caveats.
agent_relevance: Use MDL as a tie-break among comparable hypotheses, not as a general oracle.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum Description Length Revisited (prior robustness)
finding: MDL criteria are more robust than Bayesian criteria such as BDeu when the assumed prior is a poor match, staying close to Bayes with the prior adapted to the data.
numbers: Review passage on robustness; no new experiment.
limits: Review only.
agent_relevance: State the code or prior used; the length depends on it.

source: Whitney et al. (2020) Evaluating representations by the complexity of learning low-loss predictors
finding: MDL and mutual information correspond to slices and integrals along the data axis of a loss-data curve, so they measure a fixed-size dataset. Surplus description length and sample complexity fix the loss instead.
numbers: Framework with real-data experiments over varying dataset sizes.
limits: MDL ranking can depend on the evaluation dataset size.
agent_relevance: A tie-break may flip with the number of cases; do not fix a rule from one n.

source: Kaushik et al. (2023) LLaMA-7B as predictor for entropy and compression of English
finding: LLM next-token prediction plus lossless coding beats BSC, ZPAQ and paq8h in preliminary tests and gives a lower entropy bound for English.
numbers: Preliminary, limited experiments; no numbers extracted beyond the abstract.
limits: Preliminary; parameter cost not counted.
agent_relevance: Prediction equals compression; supports model loss as the data term.

source: Learning Options via Compression (2022)
finding: Adds a description-length penalty on skills to the likelihood objective in offline multi-task RL.
numbers: Authors report that skills learned with the penalty solve downstream tasks in fewer samples than likelihood-only skills; scales to image observations.
limits: No LLM; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: MDL used to choose reusable skills in an agent, an older pattern for operator libraries.

source: Compressibility Measures Complexity (2025) MDL meets Singular Learning Theory
finding: Search-result summary only: links the local learning coefficient to MDL so network complexity can be estimated beyond parameter counts.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not read in full.
agent_relevance: Parameter count is a bad proxy for model cost.
